newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - BUBA set to free repos from minimum reserves.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BUBA set to free repos from minimum reserves.

text.p: The Bundesbank is set to give Germany's lagging financial centre another boost this year by freeing securities repurchase, or repo, business from minimum reserve requirements, the bank's deputy president said.

The move would recreate a market for such commercial transactions in Germany, which has suffered an exodus of business to London because of the costs of meeting the requirements, leaving it with just weekly repo tenders for Bundesbank funds.

At present, banks in Germany must hold two percent of sight deposits and 1.5 percent of savings deposits in non-interest bearing accounts at the Bundesbank. That gives the central bank funds with which to steer money market rates.

In an interview with Boersen-Zeitung published on Tuesday, Johann Wilhelm Gaddum said he was confident the Bundesbank would decide this autumn to exempt repo business from the minimum reserve requirement.

Economists and bankers welcomed the move but said it was overdue and unlikely to prompt a repatriation of business back to Germany. Gaddum himself said in the interview one should expect "no wonders" from the exemption.
He also stressed that the Bundesbank still viewed minimum reserves as necessary.

An exemption for repos would be the latest in a series of moves aimed at getting Germany's financial centre in shape for 1999, when it will lose its main attraction -- the mark -- with the launch of the European single currency.

The Bundesbank in July gave its grudging approval to the issue of short-term government debt, and expects so-called stripping, the separate trade of principal and interest for certain bonds -- to be introduced next year.

"Better late than never," said Peter Coym, a management board member of Lehman Brothers Bankhaus AG in Frankfurt, the German arm of the U.S. investment bank, commenting on the repo move. "I think there is still a chance to build a decent repo market in Germany."
But Coym said he doubted it would be possible to lure back institutional business. It was more likely that a domestic repo market would emerge among companies, he said.

Hermann Remsperger, chief economist at BHF-Bank in Frankfurt, said, "It's good for Germany's financial centre without hurting monetary policy. It will create equal conditions for competition, which is to be welcomed."

The Bundesbank had cut the minimum reserve requirement several times and proved that it could still guide money market rates with a very low requirement, Remsperger said, adding, "I don't think this latest cut will change that."

Gaddum said the Bundesbank had conducted a detailed survey among banks this year to find out the size of banks' domestic and foreign repo business and what impact an exemption for repos would have on the minimum reserves.

The survey was aimed at establishing whether the exemption would affect the "substance of the minimum reserve" and stressed that the Bundesbank had never left any doubt that that substance should be maintained, because it was necessary.

Under a repo transaction, a dealer borrows funds from an investor by selling securities to him. The dealer repurchases the securities at a later date, thereby repaying the loan. The difference between the sale and repurchase price represents interest on the loan.
Recent comments from Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick had created the impression that Bundesbank objections to an exemption for repos had strengthened, the paper said.
Gaddum wanted to counter that impression, but he declined to reveal the findings of the survey, the paper added.
